cards.explanation: The reason the Teacher gives is that each official is watched by one higher up. He says "…one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them." (Ecclesiastes 5:8) So one official has a superior watching, and others are higher still. I think that's his way of saying: don't fall over in shock when you see this, friends.

The produce of the earth is taken by all. The Teacher says "The produce of the earth is taken by all…" (Ecclesiastes 5:9). Everybody gets a piece of it. Kind of like a fresh tray on my counter, friends: I turn around for one second and the whole tray has a crumb problem.

The answer is True. The Teacher says "the king himself profits from the fields." (Ecclesiastes 5:9) Even the guy at the very top is getting something out of that dirt. Nobody is above the harvest, friends.

The word is satisfied. "He who loves money is never satisfied by money…" (Ecclesiastes 5:10) It's like finishing a whole batch of cookies and still hunting the cooling rack for one more, friends. Having plenty and still wanting more is the whole picture.

The answer is those who consume them. The Teacher says "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). The more that comes in, the more consumers show up to use it. I've watched a cookie box do this with my own eyes.

The owner's profit is getting to look at them. The Teacher asks "what then is the profit to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes?" (Ecclesiastes 5:11) All that stuff, and the owner's profit is looking at it. That's like baking twelve dozen cookies and getting to stand there and stare.
The word is sleep. "The sleep of the worker is sweet…" (Ecclesiastes 5:12) The rich man's abundance, though, "…permits him no sleep." Honestly, friends, a good pillow beats a big pile of anything.

The answer is False. The Teacher says "The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much…" (Ecclesiastes 5:12). Little or much, the sleep is sweet either way. It's the rich man's abundance that keeps him awake.

The answer is that there is nothing to pass on. The wealth is lost in a failed venture, "…so when that man has a son there is nothing to pass on." (Ecclesiastes 5:14) The son is there, but the inheritance isn't. I think that's a heavy picture, so let's let it sit for a second.

The answer is False. The Teacher says a man came from his mother's womb, and will depart "…naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands." (Ecclesiastes 5:15) Hands empty going out, same as coming in. Nothing makes the trip.

The word is gains. The Teacher asks, "What does he gain as he toils for the wind?" (Ecclesiastes 5:16) It's a question with a pretty clear answer sitting in it. You can't hold wind, friends, and I have tried to stamp it.

He eats in darkness with much sorrow. The Teacher says "…all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger." (Ecclesiastes 5:17) I think this one hurts, friends. It's a heavy way to live, and it's the man who toils for the wind.

What's good and fitting is to eat and drink and enjoy his work. The Teacher says it's good and fitting "to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18) Enjoy the work you're given, friends. Even the stamping part, even the cleanup.

The answer is True. The Teacher speaks of "…the few days of life that God has given him…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18). Few days is a good reason to enjoy them. Nobody needs to spend those days staring at the ceiling.

The words are enjoy and gift. The Teacher says God "…has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) God does the enabling here, so the man doesn't have to squeeze the joy out of it on his own. Then the Teacher ends the verse with "This is a gift from God." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) That's good news for anybody holding a mixing spoon, friends: enjoying your work is something God gives.

The reason is that he is kept occupied with joy. The text says "For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart." (Ecclesiastes 5:20) So God is the One keeping him busy with joy. A man with a glad heart doesn't spend his days counting them.
